Silversmiths in Newburyport, Massachusetts, often crafted decorative serving pieces like this to bring traditional elegance into everyday middle-class homes. They were made during the mid-20th century to serve sweets, nuts, or small candies during formal gatherings and family celebrations. Craftsmen created these pieces by stamping base metal alloys with heavy hydraulic presses before applying a fine layer of silver plate and detailed hand-buffing. Middle-class families used them on coffee tables, sideboards, and dining tables during holidays and special visits. Over time, as formal entertaining declined and modern stainless steel became popular for daily use, these decorative silver-plated dishes transitioned from dining tables to enclosed display cabinets.

This artwork depicts the famous image of Moses and the Israelites crossing the Sea of Reeds from the Torah/Bible. The piece is a notable example of micrography —a traditional Jewish art form where intricate designs and images are created entirely out of tiny, handwritten text. This specific piece is uniquely crafted using the entire Hebrew text of the Book of Exodus (Hebrew: Shmot ) to form the shapes of the parted waves, the gathering crowd, and the landscape.
